height_m_by_age.source: Silvics of North America,     Pinus ponderosa (Oliver and Ryker 1990) site curves after Meyer 1938,     read as site index about 100 ft at 100 y for the lower Sierra edge: 12 m at 25 y,     25 at 60,     35 at 110,     42 at 300; the record's 22-38 m. Not fitted to measurements

dbh_cm_by_age.source: Tallo's California ponderosas (n 62,     H = 1.023 dbh^0.80,     fit 2026-11-01) inverted on the height curve: 27 cm at 25 y,     53 at 60,     76 at 110,     107 at 300

crown_width_m_by_dbh_cm.source: Bechtold 2004 table 3,     ponderosa pine (n 1413): LCW ft = 2.3089 + 1.1388 dbh in - 0.0089 dbh in^2; a check,     not an input. Tallo (n 448 crowned): W/H 0.49 at 5-10 m,     0.35 at 15-20,     0.23 at 25-30,     0.21 at 30-40; times 1.2 open-grown: the Urban Tree Database's open street ponderosas at 14-16 y are 3-7 m wide against Bechtold's 3.9 at their dbh

wood.source: Wood Handbook FPL-GTR-190 table 5-3a,     ponderosa pine green: specific gravity 0.38,     modulus 6.9 GPa (8.9 at 12 %); green density from 0.38 at about 90 % moisture

description: A tall,     straight pine with a clear trunk,     thick bark broken into cinnamon-orange plates between black fissures,     and long needles (12-25 cm,     in threes) in tufts at the branch tips; 22-38 m tall here. It grows above the oak woodland in the lower conifer forest,     from about 600 m up,     and its thick bark lets old trees survive the frequent low fires that once kept these forests open.

season_notes.winter: Evergreen: needles stay on for about three years,     so the crown is full in every season.
season_notes.spring: Pollen cones release clouds of yellow pollen (May-June) and new shoots extend at the branch tips.
season_notes.summer: Second-year seed cones grow to full size and turn from green to red-brown.
season_notes.fall: Cones open and drop winged seeds (September-October) for squirrels,     chipmunks and birds; the oldest needles yellow and fall.

targets.from: reference photographs,     docs/tree-likeness-review.md: 02,     03 mature (clear bole 40-60%),     04 old flat top (crown porosity 0.14); young trees are conical to the ground

notes: The dominant pine of the lower montane conifer forest above the foothills. Mature trees here 22-38 m (to 70 m elsewhere),     dbh 0.6-1.2 m (dbh/height about 0.03),     with a tall,     straight,     barely tapering trunk clear of branches for nearly half its height (bole_ratio and base_size 0.45; lower limbs self-prune). Excurrent Rauh's model: the leader runs to the top (length_ratio 1,     taper 1) and level-1 branches are whorled (about three per visible whorl in old trees),     roughly horizontal: the lowest droop slightly below horizontal (98 degrees) and arch down and turn up again at the tips (droop_deg 34 over the inner half,     upturn_deg 40 over the outer half,     because in-world review found the limbs too straight),     the upper ones ascend (58 degrees). Old crowns are open,     narrowly rounded to flat-topped,     hence the tapered_cylindrical shape (long branches persist near the top). Bark of mature 'yellow pine' is the signature: thick cinnamon-orange plates separated by deep black fissures ('plates' pattern); young trees ('blackjacks') are dark. Needles 12-25 cm in bundles of three,     dark yellow-green,     held in dense brush-like tufts at the ends of the twigs,     so level-2 twigs carry only foliage (near_sides 0). Foliage: needle_brush cards,     each a branch end with four or five upturned shoots forking wide,     each ending in a round starburst tuft of needle bundles,     drawn as two crossed planes through the shoot (needle_planes 2) and turned up (tuft_up); clumps of two cards on the outer part of each limb (level-2 start 0.5,     parent_start 0.6),     so the crown is open inside. Colour recalibrated to the photo ratios (r/g 0.95,     b/g 0.47 in linear light). Needle light (canopyMaterial): each needle's own normal mixed into the crown normal (needle_normal),     wrap lighting (needle_wrap),     light through thin needle edges when the sun is behind (translucency) and a weak glow of the whole backlit crown (needle_scatter).
sources: Oliver and Ryker 1990,     Silvics of North America vol. 1,     Pinus ponderosa
Halle,     Oldeman and Tomlinson 1978 (Rauh's model; Pinus as example)
